chapter_theme: Neythal in the time of the secret love: the man is struck at first sight by the fisher's daughter guarding drying fish (32, 33, 45, 47); the friend bars the night shore of sharks and wave-elephants, closes the day to gossip and presses for marriage (34-37, 43, 44, 46); the girl laments to the sleepless sea, to the crab and her own melting heart once he has gone (38, 40-42).

32.reading: The man says that the girl set to guard the drying fish that her brothers, knowing the fishing grounds of the cool backwater of blue lilies, scooped up with nets of fine thread, turns on him the look of her long, weapon-like eyes: the guarding is cruel, and it is he, not the fish, whom she holds.
32.nuance: The verb காப்பு plays on her task: she is set to guard the fish from birds, and the guard her eyes keep falls on the onlooker instead, so the shore chore becomes the first-sight scene. கடிபொல்லா is hard; 'the guarding is cruel' is the reading taken here.

thinai_evidence.note: the netted fish drying on the shore grove and the fishing kin are neythal things

comparisons.tenor: her long eyes, whose look wounds like a weapon

33.reading: The man says that seeing the white smile, like the pearls of the dark sea, of the sister of those who dive into the vast sea for the white conch without a thought for themselves, his heart has become like theirs, melting and wasting away.
33.nuance: The brothers neglect their lives diving for the sea's white conch; the speaker, drawn by the sea's other white thing in her smile, says he has become one of those who melt and waste, so the kin's trade and the lover's ruin are set side by side without a marker.

thinai_evidence.note: the conch-divers of the great sea are neythal people and things

34.reading: The friend tells the lord of the cool expanse, whose backwater sleeps with the lotus for its face and the great blue lily among cool leaves for its lovely eyes, that if he comes in the spreading dark he will find the girl of the hanging garland melting in tears, her eyes stretched wide along the way.
34.nuance: The backwater, given a lotus face and lily eyes, sleeps; the girl, whose own face and eyes those flowers stand for, does not. காணீர் can be read as 'you will see' or 'you will not see', which turns the line into a warning or a reproach.

thinai_evidence.note: the cool sea expanse and the night of waiting fix the shore

comparisons.tenor: the blue lily among the leaves

35.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore of swelling water, where the flowering punnai drives off the smell of fish and the white sand of the cool grove outshines the moon, not to come in the night, and warns that if he comes by day there will be talk by the white waves in the mist, so that neither way is left open to him.
35.nuance: Shutting both the night tryst and the day tryst is the friend's way of leaving marriage as the only road; the poem does not say so, and the closing lines are obscure (சுலா அகற்றி, மார்க்).

thinai_evidence.note: the flowering punnai and the shore grove are neythal things

iraicchi.act: the heron feeds what it takes for its chick and shades it from the sun with its wings
iraicchi.sense: even a bird keeps steady, self-forgetting care for what it holds as its own, so the hero should stop coming and going and marry her

36.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, where a heron, taking the long bud of the fragrant thorny screwpine for its chick, puts food to it, and when it will not eat, melts and shades it with its wings from the cruel sun, to give up these coming-and-going visits.
36.nuance: மன்னா வரவு, a coming that does not stay, is the point of the image: the bird gives unbroken care even to what only looks like its young, while the hero comes and goes.

thinai_evidence.note: the screwpine and the shore heron are neythal things

37.reading: The friend tells the hero that the people of the tide-fenced hamlet, who never hold back their talk, keep their eyes on his comings for love, and only the tide knew of that first day; so, rather than coming in secret, let him marry her for the common square to know, and the gossip will end.
37.nuance: The tide appears twice, once as the fence of the gossiping hamlet and once as the only witness of the secret union; the friend sets the witness that cannot speak against the town that will not stop speaking, and asks for the square (மன்று) to become the witness instead.

thinai_evidence.note: a hamlet fenced by the tide is the neythal shore

38.reading: The girl, kept awake because the breast of the lord of the cool expanse has afflicted her, asks the great sea, which like her does not sleep, who has done this to it, and whether it too suffers a grief like hers.
38.nuance: The addressee is the sea. The question 'who did this to you' answers itself in the first two lines, which name who did it to her: she reads her own cause into the sea's restlessness.

thinai_evidence.note: the sleepless lament addressed to the sea is neythal's irangal

comparisons.tenor: the sea that does not sleep

39.reading: The friend says the broad soft shoulders belong only to the one who gave himself to her, and she will see whether those who say they will go to whoever comes asking on such a day are speaking true; for the one who came, there is the young njaazhal of the cool backwater grove, unguarded and not yet in flower.
39.nuance: The unguarded, unopened njaazhal bud, kept for the one who came, may stand for the girl already promised to her lover; it gives only one pair, so it is not tagged as ullurai. The verse reads like the friend's disclosure to the household when another suitor is spoken of, but the addressee is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the njaazhal of the backwater grove is a neythal tree

iraicchi.act: the crab plays with its mate
iraicchi.sense: even the crab keeps its partner at play beside it, while the man who should have stayed has gone

40.reading: The girl says that, watching the crab play with its mate, she asked whether she might play with her own sweet companion; and he said, 'if you have played with your sweet companion, why grieve over that ache?', and went away, set on going.
40.nuance: His reply turns her own word இன்துணை back on her: the pleasure is already had, so the ache is not his to answer for. Who speaks the second half is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore crab with its mate is a neythal creature

41.reading: The girl says her heart melts, and not for one day only, while the talk about them swells, and she loosens like the cloud that draws close, gathered with lightning and thunder, and pours.
41.nuance: The rain-cloud carries both halves of the first two lines: the heart that melts and the talk that swells (பெருகுமால்) gather together in one storm. பேண and பெருகா ஒருங்குவால் are uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: melting under the town's talk is the lament of irangal; nothing in the verse names a shore

comparisons.tenor: her melting heart and the swelling talk

42.reading: Like the great elephant, heavy with its mouthfuls, that cannot hold its ground when a young aali crawls near, her bangles will not stay on her arms each time she sees pearls set among the coral beads, and pearl-like tears gather in her hands.
42.nuance: The elephant and the aali belong to the hills; the poet borrows them for a sea-shore girl. The line division is unsure: முத்தம் in line 4 may be the pearls of her ornament or her tears, and the speaker is not named.

thinai_evidence.note: coral and pearl are things of the sea shore

comparisons.tenor: her bangles, which will not stay on her thinning arms
the tears gathering in her hands

43.reading: The friend tells the lord of the long shore, where the waves become a fierce tusked elephant, with the sea's two horns for tusks and the wind for its mahout, and rage and leap upon the bank, not to come in the thick dark, but to come as one who will marry her.
43.nuance: The danger of the night shore is drawn as a war elephant under a mahout; the wind drives the waves as the mahout drives the beast, so the image says the danger is steered, not random. கடற்கோடு, 'the sea's horns', is unclear: it may be the conch or the crests.

thinai_evidence.note: the wave-beaten shore at night is the neythal setting

comparisons.tenor: the waves that the wind drives against the shore

44.reading: The friend tells the lord of the ford, where the punnai drives off the strong fish smell, that the place of the simple doe-eyed girl, who went in to chase the birds from the drying fish, is the broad grove grown thick and tall with screwpine and njaazhal.
44.nuance: Naming the grove where the girl does her daily task is how the friend fixes a day meeting without saying so.

thinai_evidence.note: punnai, drying fish, screwpine and njaazhal are neythal things

45.reading: The friend says that, having seen the large broad eyes, matchless though one searched every land, of the simple young daughter of the fisherfolk on the cool grove of white sand where the screwpine creeps, he sought her as his partner, and is without fault.
45.nuance: துணை நாடினன் may be a plea for the hero: he wants her as a wife, not a passing love. The speaker and addressee are inferred, and மாழை and தோம் இலன் can be read otherwise.

thinai_evidence.note: the screwpine and the fisherfolk are neythal things

46.reading: The friend tells the hero that there is no need to bring gifts and search: if he asks for her one day and comes without delay, he will win her by word alone; but, my lord, the girl of the long makara earrings will not live if he comes in the night when the striking shark circles, so let him not come.
46.nuance: The same word மகரம் is the ornament on her ear and the beast in the sea: what adorns her is what threatens him, and the friend's fear is for both. தந்து ஆயல் is unsure.

thinai_evidence.note: the shark of the night sea is a neythal creature

47.reading: The man says that in the backwater grove where bees sing tunes nobody set, she is a beauty that strikes like a goddess those who look without thinking, and her kin, whose courage never flags though they die without a thought, do not guard her: they have slipped the rope and let her loose.
47.nuance: Her kin let her roam like a beast untied, which is a complaint about the danger she poses, not about her safety. Whether the 'courage that does not flag though dying' belongs to the kin or to the lovesick onlookers is unclear.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater grove is the neythal setting

comparisons.tenor: her beauty, which seizes the onlooker

links.note: Kural 1085 finds death, an eye and a doe in the young woman's look; Thinaimalai 32 calls the fish-guard's long eyes a weapon (படைநெடுங்கண்) whose guarding falls on the man.
links.teaches: The couplet lists in the abstract what a first look can be, and the poem supplies the scene that makes 'death' concrete: a girl posted to guard the drying fish whose watch is turned on the man who looks, so the Kural's killing glance is a guard's weapon.

links.note: 32 is the man's first sight of the girl guarding the drying fish; 44 has the friend name the grove of that same task as the girl's place.
links.teaches: Read together the two verses show the fish-drying watch doing for the neythal girl what the millet watch does in kurinji: it is where the man first sees her and, later, the daytime meeting place the friend appoints.

links.note: Akananuru 80: the friend says they spend the day driving birds from their father's drying fish and bids him come by day to the punnai grove; Thinaimalai 44 names the grove where the girl went to drive birds from the drying fish (புட்கடிவான் புக்க).
links.teaches: The long poem spells out the trade behind the short one: naming the grove where the girl chases birds from the fish is the friend's way of replacing the dangerous night swim with a day meeting, which Thinaimalai 44 implies but never states.

links.note: Akananuru 80 forbids the night swim and offers a day meeting in the punnai grove; Thinaimalai 35 forbids the night and warns that a day visit brings gossip.
links.teaches: Set beside Akananuru 80, where the day meeting is the friend's remedy for the night's danger, Thinaimalai 35 shows a later stage in which the day too is closed by gossip, so that the only road left is marriage.

links.note: Both use a shore bird that takes something else for a heron's chick: in Ainkurunuru 151 a stork treads a neythal flower going to see it; in Thinaimalai 36 a heron feeds a screwpine bud and shades it with its wings.
links.teaches: The same mistake of a bird taking a flower for a chick can carry opposite senses: in Ainkurunuru the error bruises the flower, which still gives off scent, like the heroine who stays tender to the man who hurt her, while in Thinaimalai it becomes devoted care held up to shame a man whose visits do not stay.

links.note: Kuruntokai 25: no one but the man was there, only a heron watching for fish, on the day he took her; Thinaimalai 37: the tide knew it that day (ஓதநீர் அன்றறியும்), so marry her before the common square.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai's girl fears that a union witnessed only by a shore creature leaves her helpless if he lies, and Thinaimalai's friend answers that fear: a witness that cannot speak is why the union must be made public in the square.

links.note: Kuruntokai 163 asks the sea who has afflicted it (யாரணங் குற்றனை) since she hears it even at midnight; Thinaimalai 38 asks the sleepless sea who did this to it, 'like me'.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai leaves the girl's own state unsaid behind her question to the sea, while Thinaimalai 38 names it, the breast of the shore lord and a sleeplessness 'like mine', so the pair shows the later poet making explicit the projection the older poem left to the hearer.

links.note: In Akananuru 380 the man shows the girls a crab carrying a naaval fruit to its mate and says 'this is a fine way'; in Thinaimalai 40 the girl watches a crab playing with its mate after the man has left.
links.teaches: The crab with its mate is the shore lover's own emblem of devotion, used by the man in Akananuru 380 to court the girl; Thinaimalai 40 shows the emblem turned against him, watched by the girl alone after he dismissed her ache and went.

links.note: Kural 1147: the sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and the mother's words as water; Thinaimalai 41: the heart melts day after day while the talk swells, like a storm cloud pouring.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the gossip the food of the love-sickness, and Thinaimalai 41 makes the two one weather, the swelling talk and the melting heart pouring together like a cloud, which shows the girl suffering the growth the couplet describes as a cause.

links.note: In Natrinai 287 the girl says he came unafraid of the dread crocodile of the backwater; in Thinaimalai 46 the friend bars him from the night when the striking shark circles.
links.teaches: The night beast of the backwater counts for the girl in Natrinai 287 as the proof of his love and for the friend in Thinaimalai 46 as the reason to stop him and ask for marriage, so the same danger is read by each speaker to serve her own aim.

links.note: Kural 1081: the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess (அணங்கு), a peahen or a woman; Thinaimalai 47: she is a beauty that strikes like a goddess (ஏரணங்கு) those who look without thinking.
links.teaches: The Kural's man hesitates over what she is, while the Thinaimalai speaker has settled it and turns to blame, saying her kin have let such a danger loose unguarded, so the pair shows the first-sight wonder of the couplet hardening into a lover's complaint.

source_issues: 32-47: the core records carry no colophon thurai, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.
35: flagged as a different verse from the site's 35 (similarity 0.19); சுலா அகற்றி and மார்க் in lines 3 are obscure as printed.
32 line 4: கடிபொல்லா is hard to divide; read as கடி பொல்லா, 'the guarding is cruel'.
39: the whole verse is obscure; the division of lines 1-2 (தந்தார்க்கே ஆம், வந்தார்க்கே ஆம்) is uncertain.
42: line 1 களிப்பியனமால் and the division of lines 3-4 (கடிகை யிடைமுத்தம், தொடிகை யிடைமுத்தம்) are uncertain.
43 line 1: கடற்கோ(டு) is unclear (the sea's horns, perhaps conch or crests).
44 line 4: எழைமான் is probably ஏழை மான் (as ஏழை in 45 line 2).
47: பண்மேல்தே is read as பண் மேல் தே(ன்), the bee; the subject of சாவார் சான்றாண்மை is unclear.
Editorial bracketed letters (பேணா(து), பெய்(து), மார்(பு), ஓ(டு)) are kept as printed.
